title: GPU hotspot scan: ephemeral warp bursts and scheduling gaps
content:
Status / summary:

Short: ran focused Nsight Systems + Nsight Compute sweeps to characterize short-duration SM activity spikes we observed during streaming generation. Found recurring sub-100ms warp-level bursts ('ephemeral warps') that coincide with kernel launch boundaries and async-copy scheduling, creating periodic SM idling and downstream tail-latency variance.

Goal / motivation:
- Reproduce and root-cause intermittent latency spikes (+10-40ms tail) seen in nightly production traces when serving mid-length sequences (seq_len 512, batch=1..4).
- Identify whether spikes are due to kernel launch serialization, CUDA graph fragmentation, host-side enqueue jitter, or memory copy phasing.
- Produce mitigation ideas that don't require model architecture changes (scheduling and runtime-level fixes preferred).

Environment / config:
- HW: NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB (2-socket cluster test node with single GPU used for traces)
- CUDA: 11.8, cuBLAS/cuDNN: system-provided, driver 535.xx
- Runtime: serving-runtime v0.24.1-nightly (custom build with debug symbols), allocator=tensor-pool, kv-cache enabled
- Model: llama-7b-32k-quant (runtime variant r7b-q4f), generation params: temperature=0.2, top_p=0.95, max_new_tokens=256
- Workload: steady stream of single-request chat generation from benchmark harness (qps 4, interarrival jitter ~5-20ms)

Tracing commands and notes:
- High-level trace for correlation:
  nsys profile --output=nsys-hotspot-2026-03-15 --trace=nvtx,cuda,osrt --capture-range=none --stop-on-range-end true 
    --sample=cpu --duration=120s --env="NSYS_NVTX_ENABLE=1" 
    -- python3 perf_harness/streaming_client.py --model r7b-q4f --qps 4 --duration 90

- Per-kernel microprofiling (hot kernels identified from nsys):
  ncu --target-processes all --set full --metrics sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed,sm__pipe_tensor_cycles_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed,sm__warps_launched_per_cycle.avg 
    --session-profile ncu-ephemeral-2026-03-15 ./bin/serving-runtime --config debug-local.yaml

- Lightweight periodic snapshot to measure async memcpy phasing: added host timestamps around device-to-host enqueue points and captured queue depths.

Observations (what the traces show):
1) Repro pattern: every ~60-140ms there is a cluster of tiny kernels (few ms each) that launch in quick succession, separated by 1-3ms gaps of near-zero SM utilization. The cluster itself corresponds to attention/kcache updates + small utility kernels.

2) Warp-level metric behavior: NCU shows sm__warps_launched_per_cycle spikes to ~0.9 then drops to 0.02 in the gaps. Tensor pipe cycles active metric indicates high utilization only during the micro-kernels; aggregate per-kernel occupancy is high, but system-wide occupancy averaged across time is low because of gaps.

3) CUDA graph fragmentation: these micro-kernels are scheduled as multiple nodes in a captured CUDA graph. The graph we build at runtime splits the forward pass into ~12 nodes for kcache+attention+ffn. The driver replays nodes sequentially; when nodes are short (<4ms) the overhead of node boundary transitions and stream synchronization becomes visible.

4) Host-side enqueue jitter: the harness uses a single host thread to enqueue tasks into the CUDA graph; jitter in the event loop (python GC spikes + scheduler) can increase time between graph node submissions in graphs not fully captured for replay, which exacerbates gaps.

5) Async copy phasing: in some runs D2H copies are spilled to default stream due to a fallback path for small scratch buffers (legacy code path). Those copies sometimes preempt tensor-kernel streams, causing short interruptions.

Representative timeline (simplified):
- 0 ms: kernel A (attention chunk) runs, SM util 85% for 3.4ms
- 3.4 - 5.2 ms: gap, SM util ~5% (wait + serialization)
- 5.2 ms: kernel B (kv update) runs 2.1ms, util 80%
- 7.3 - 8.6 ms: nanogap (cuda graph node transition)
- 8.6 ms: small kernel C (softmax) runs 1.6ms
- ... repeat every token prefix boundary

Key hypothesis (why the bursts happen):
- Short kernels combined with graph-node transitions and occasional host-side scheduling jitter produce effective serialization. The driver/RT overhead at node boundaries plus fallback memcpy interference creates wall-clock gaps despite high per-kernel occupancy.

Quick experiments and their findings:
- Experiment: Merge nodes in the capture (restructure graph to combine attention+kcache short kernels into a single node). Result: reduced gap frequency and 30-45% decrease in tail latency. However, merging increases single-node memory working set and slightly raises peak memory footprint (~4-6%).

- Experiment: Switch D2H copies to a dedicated high-priority stream and use cudaMemcpyAsync pinned buffers. Result: eliminated a subset of long gaps; tail improved ~12% on runs where D2H fallback previously fired.

- Experiment: Activate 'persistent-kernel' skeleton for token-loop (one persistent kernel that services token generation). Result: best tail improvement (~50% reduction in 95/99p for single-GPU test), but requires larger refactor and is sensitive to debug/kill semantics. Also blocked by current allocator assumptions.

- Experiment: Introduced micro-batching (accumulate 2 tokens before launching). Result: smoother SM utilization and fewer gaps at cost of slight added latency for first tokens in a generation; good trade for mid-throughput tiers.

Actionable mitigations (ranked):
1) Short-term (low-risk): Ensure all D2H/D2D copies use pinned buffers + dedicated async copy streams (high-priority) and audit fallback code paths. Patch in next-week hotfix.

2) Medium-term (moderate effort): Merge graph nodes at capture time using heuristics (if kernel runtime < 5ms, try to coalesce neighboring nodes). Add an opt-in capture flag. This reduces node-boundary overhead without moving to persistent kernels.

3) Long-term (higher effort): Implement persistent-kernel event loop for token stepping. Requires allocator changes and careful cleanup logic, but yields best tail predictability. Consider as opt-in mode for Dedicated customers.

4) Runtime scheduler improvements: Add a small host-side jitter-tolerant enqueue buffer or a dedicated enqueue thread pinned to isolated CPU core (avoids GC and scheduler preemption impacts).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How often does the D2H fallback path trigger in production vs test (need sampling from prod traces INF-logs)? Add telemetry to emit a counter when fallback is used.
- Validate memory overhead of node merging across large models (7b vs 70b), run a memory-pressure sweep.
- Explore combining node-merging heuristic with adaptive microbatching (auto-toggle based on recent tail-latency).

Notes to self / team TODOs:
- [INF-2387] attach nsys trace + trimmed timeline snippet to ticket (Aisha)
- Add a unit test that asserts no fallback memcpy path for pinned buffers (Diego)
- PoC branch for node-coalescing heuristics: runtime/graph-coalesce-proto (Marcus)
- Run nightly sweep on dedicated cluster with larger sequence lengths (1k+) and capture 24h traces (Sylvia)

Appendix: quick shell snippets collected during run
- Extract hot kernel list from nsys summary: 
  nsys stats nsys-hotspot-2026-03-15.qdrep | grep -E "CUDA_KERNEL|Name" -n

- Minimal repro harness invocation (local):
  python3 perf_harness/streaming_client.py --model r7b-q4f --qps 4 --duration 120 --capture-nsys nsys-hotspot-2026-03-15

- Lightweight python timepoint patch used to correlate host enqueue jitter:
  # in request_loop.py
  t_enqueue_submit = time.time()
  stream.submit_graph(graph)
  t_post_submit = time.time()
  metrics.emit("enqueue_delta_ms", (t_post_submit - t_enqueue_submit)*1000)

Closing note: This scan gave a clearer story: per-kernel occupancy is not the issue; it's fragmentation and scheduling boundaries. Short kernels + graph-node boundaries + occasional D2H fallback == ephemeral warp bursts + idle gaps. Recommend landing the pinned-copy hotfix and prototyping node coalescing next sprint.

If we want to present this to infra/product: prepare short demo that shows before/after nsys timelines (merged node vs baseline) and a small table with 50/95/99p latencies for baseline / pinned-copy / node-merge / persistent-kernel.
